title: Proving who you are
syllabusUnit: Unit IV: User Authentication & Password Security
covers: Passwords, biometrics, challenge-response, password hashing (salt, Argon2)
learningGoals: You will be able to explain why databases must store salted, slow hashes (Argon2, bcrypt) instead of plain SHA-256.
You will be able to describe how Challenge-Response prevents password replay attacks.
You will be able to evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of Biometric authentication.

lessonCards.title: The Password Salt & Slow Hashing
lessonCards.analogy: Sprinkling random seasoning onto every dish so even identical recipes produce totally different meals.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Never hash passwords with fast hashes (SHA-256 is designed to be fast, making brute-force easy). Use slow, memory-hard key derivation functions like Argon2 or bcrypt with a unique Salt.
lessonCards.example: A 16-byte random salt defeats pre-computed rainbow table databases.

lessonCards.title: Challenge-Response Authentication
lessonCards.analogy: A sentry yells 'Thunder!' You reply 'Flash!' You prove you know the password without shouting it out loud.
lessonCards.coreConcept: The server issues a random challenge Nonce R. The client replies with Response = H(Password || R). The server verifies the match without the password ever traveling across the wire.
lessonCards.example: An eavesdropper capturing the response cannot reuse it because the next challenge will be totally different.

lessonCards.title: Biometrics: What You Are
lessonCards.analogy: Your face or thumbprint is your username, not your secret key: you cannot change your thumbprint if it gets leaked.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Biometrics (fingerprint, FaceID, iris) measure physical traits. They provide high convenience and non-transferability, but false acceptance rates and revocability limitations require secure hardware enclaves.
lessonCards.example: Fingerprint templates are stored as fuzzy mathematical hashes in device Secure Elements, never sent to cloud servers.

questions.prompt: Why is hashing passwords with plain SHA-256 or MD5 considered a severe security vulnerability?
options: Fast general-purpose hashes can be brute-forced at billions of guesses per second using consumer GPUs
MD5 makes database files too large
questions.explanation: Modern graphics cards test over 10 billion SHA-256 hashes per second. Password storage requires slow, memory-hard algorithms like Argon2id or bcrypt.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Fast hashing enables rapid offline brute-force and dictionary attacks.
SHA-256 processes arbitrary text strings.
MD5 output is only 16 bytes.
SHA-256 handles all binary data.
questions.realWorldExample: In the 2012 LinkedIn breach, 117 million unsalted SHA-1 password hashes were cracked in days.

questions.prompt: What is the primary cryptographic purpose of adding a unique 'Salt' to every password before hashing?
options: To defeat pre-computed Rainbow Table lookup dictionaries and ensure identical passwords have different hashes
To encrypt the database hard drive
questions.explanation: A random salt ensures that if two users choose 'password123', their stored database hashes are totally different, forcing attackers to crack each user individually.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Salt forces attackers to compute separate dictionaries for every single user.
Full-disk encryption uses BitLocker or LUKS.
Salting lengthens the hashed input string.
Languages are unchanged.
questions.realWorldExample: A standard salt is at least 16 random bytes stored alongside the hash in the database.

questions.prompt: Which modern password hashing algorithm was the winner of the Password Hashing Competition (PHC) and is recommended by OWASP?
questions.explanation: Argon2 provides configurable execution time, memory hardness, and parallel thread cost to resist GPU and ASIC attacks.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Argon2id is the state-of-the-art memory-hard password hashing standard.
SHA-1 is deprecated and broken.
DES is an obsolete block cipher.
Rot13 is a toy Caesar shift by 13.
questions.realWorldExample: Argon2 was selected as the winner of the international Password Hashing Competition in 2015.

questions.prompt: In a challenge-response authentication protocol, why can't an attacker replay the captured response to log in later?
options: The server generates a fresh, unique random challenge (nonce) for every single authentication attempt
The server powers off after every login
Responses are encrypted by the monitor
questions.explanation: Because the server issues a new random nonce R every time, an old response computed over a previous nonce will be rejected immediately.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Nonce freshness prevents replay attacks across the wire.
Servers remain continuously online.
User passwords remain fixed unless manually reset.
Display hardware does not perform network crypto.
questions.realWorldExample: Kerberos, CHAP (Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol), and WebAuthn rely on challenge-response.

questions.prompt: What is a major inherent drawback of biometric authentication compared to passwords or hardware tokens?
options: Biometrics cannot be revoked or changed if compromised (you cannot issue yourself a new fingerprint)
questions.explanation: If a database of thumbprint or iris scans is leaked, users cannot change their biometric features like they can reset a password.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Biometrics are permanent identifiers that cannot be re-issued upon breach.
Optical and capacitive sensors work in total darkness.
Local authentication occurs completely offline on the device.
Modern phone sensors unlock in under 200 milliseconds.
questions.realWorldExample: In 2015, the US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) breach exposed 5.6 million federal employee fingerprint records.

questions.prompt: What are the three classic authentication factors defined in identity security?
options: Something you know (password), something you have (phone/token), something you are (biometrics)
First name, last name, and middle name
Browser, operating system, and IP address
questions.explanation: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) requires proof from at least two distinct categories: Knowledge, Possession, and Inherence.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Knowledge (passwords), Possession (tokens), and Inherence (biometrics).
Profile fields are public knowledge.
Names are public information.
Device fingerprints can be spoofed.
questions.realWorldExample: Enforcing MFA blocks over 99% of automated account takeover attacks according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

ashRecap: Never store plain passwords! Always use slow, salted hashes like Argon2, and add a second factor like an authenticator token to stay safe!
